Title: A Study of High Performance Dividers

Abstract: This paper explores the design of a high performance divider aimed at improving 
the performance of integer and floating point division operations to enhance the overall 
performance of the microprocessor. In the field of high-performance computing (HPC) and 
scientific computing, the design of floating-point divisors is critical because division is one 
of the most complex operations in floating-point arithmetic. The article firstly introduces the 
standard and arithmetic rules of floating-point numbers, analyses the basic principles of 
floating-point division, and compares the advantages and disadvantages of several classical 
floating-point division algorithms. In particular, the design of a double-precision floating-
point divider based on Goldschmidt's algorithm is investigated in order to solve the problem 
of the complexity of the double-precision floating-point division arithmetic process and the 
large delay. The article also discusses current technology trends and practical application 
requirements for high-performance divider design, including applications in digital signal 
processing, communication systems, image processing, and other fields. In addition, the 
article discusses key factors such as the selection of the initial value of the iteration, the 
determination of the number of iterations, and the error control, and evaluates the advantages 
and disadvantages of different hardware implementations such as the SRT algorithm, the 
CORDIC algorithm, and the Radix-8 algorithm. Finally, the article looks at future trends in 
high-performance dividers, including the application of new materials and processes, the 
development of novel algorithms, and the integration of hardware accelerators. 
Keywords: High Performance Dividers, Goldschmidt algorithm,SRT algorithm, CORDIC 
algorithm, Hardware implementation. 
1. 
Introduction 
In the field of high-performance computing and scientific computing, the performance of floating-
point dividers is critical, as it is directly related to the accuracy and stability of the system. As 
technology advances, the requirements for processor performance are no longer limited to speed, but 
also include power consumption and chip area. The aim of this paper is to provide an overview of the 
current technology and application requirements for the design of high-performance dividers, and to 
explore optimization options to advance the technology and meet practical applications. Tingting He, 
in their study proposed a high performance double precision floating point divider design based on 
Goldschmidt algorithm [1]. This study significantly improves the performance and accuracy of the 
divider by optimizing the iterative process and error control mechanism. The design and

Ziyao Deng [2].This research reduces the number of iterations and increases the speed of computation 
through parallel processing techniques and algorithm optimization, while reducing the hardware 
resource requirements. Jingcun Wang and Yingbo Wang implemented the FPGA design of a complex 
divider based on CORDIC algorithm [3].This study utilizes the CORDIC algorithm's rotation 
operation to replace the traditional multiplication and addition operations, reducing hardware 
resource consumption and increasing the speed of operations. Xujun Li, Na Shi and Kejun Long 
proposed the design of an exact floating-point divider based on polynomial approximation algorithm 
[4].The design achieves a highly accurate division operation with an error of less than 0.5 ULP by 
reducing the number of iterations and optimizing the hardware structure. These research cases 
demonstrate the diversity and activity in the field of high-performance divider design, and also point 
to directions for future research, including the application of new materials and processes, the 
development of novel algorithms, and the integration of hardware accelerators. 
This paper will analyze the strengths and limitations of different division algorithms and evaluate 
their advantages and disadvantages in terms of hardware implementation with a view to providing 
guidance for design. Through these studies, it is hoped to provide insight into the future development 
of high-performance dividers, as well as technical support for practical applications. 
2. 
Technological developments 
In the early days, the design of the divider was mainly focused on the optimization of the algorithm. 
For example, the Newton-Raphson algorithm and the Goldschmidt algorithm are two commonly used 
iterative algorithms that reduce the number of computations by iterative approximation, thus 
increasing speed. However, these algorithms still face challenges in hardware implementation, 
especially in terms of area and power consumption constraints. So modern algorithms were derived. 
Goldschmidt's algorithm is an iterative based floating point division algorithm which reduces the 
number of computations by iterative approximation. The advantage of this algorithm is that it enables 
high-speed floating-point division, but its disadvantage is that it requires a large look-up table and a 
complex error control mechanism. The SRT (Sh Subbase Radix) algorithm is an efficient numerical 
division algorithm that reduces the number of iterations by choosing a suitable base. The advantages 
of the SRT algorithm are simple hardware implementation and low area and power consumption, but 
its disadvantage is that it may require larger hardware resources in some cases. The design of a 
floating point divider based on logarithmic conversion makes use of logarithmic and antilogarithm 
conversions to simplify the division operation. The advantage of this approach is that it can 
significantly reduce the computational complexity. But the disadvantage is that it requires accurate 
logarithmic and inverse logarithmic tables. These may increase the demand on hardware resources. 
3. 
Key design and implementation factors 
The choice of the initial value of the iteration has an important impact on the convergence speed and 
final accuracy of the divider. For example, Tingting He mentioned the double lookup table method 
for determining the initial value of iteration in a double-precision floating-point divider based on 
Goldschmidt's algorithm, which saves area and improves the speed of iteration [5].In addition, the 
improved Goldschmidt algorithm in which a linear minimax polynomial approximation algorithm 
obtains an estimate of the reciprocal of the divisor with higher accuracy further optimizes the choice 
of the initial value of the iteration. The determination of the number of iterations is another key factor 
that affects the performance of the divider. Too many iterations increase the computation time, while 
not enough iterations may lead to insufficient accuracy. For example, in the design of a divider based 
on the SRT algorithm, by optimizing the algorithm structure and parallel processing techniques, the

number of iterations required can be effectively reduced, thus increasing the speed of operation. Error 
control is an important aspect of ensuring the performance of the divider. In Goldschmidt's algorithm, 
Tingting He found that the error generated during the iteration process can be effectively reduced and 
the accuracy of the calculation results can be ensured by a reasonable error control method [6].In 
addition, the optimization algorithm of the Newton iterative method also has a fast convergence rate 
with high accuracy, which helps to control the error. The SRT algorithm (Suan-Tung-Robust) is an 
efficient floating-point division algorithm widely used in modern computer systems. The algorithm 
increases the speed of the division operation by generating multiple quotient bits per iteration. To 
reduce the computational delay, the SRT algorithm can be implemented by processing quotient 
selection and remainder addition in parallel. For example, the design of SIMD structure based on 
SRT-8 algorithm mentioned by Ziyang Deng significantly reduces the computational delay and 
improves the frequency of iterative division by parallel processing of quotient selection and residue 
addition, as well as the use of the quotient digital storage technique. The performance of the SRT 
algorithm is affected by the size of the base [7].A larger base reduces the number of iterations and 
thus speeds up the computation, but at the same time increases the hardware complexity and area. For 
example, the optimization method proposed by Huaping Liu achieves a reduction in latency, albeit 
with an increase in area, for SRT algorithms with different bases, such as bases 4, 8, and 16, by 
executing in parallel two relatively independent parts of the traditional SRT structure (calculating the 
input values of the selection function table and finding the selection function table) [8].To reduce the 
overhead of hardware resources and save area, multiplexing strategies can be used. For example, the 
design mentioned by Jiyang Chen reduces hardware resource overhead by multiplexing lookup tables 
and adders, while reducing computational latency through parallel processing and on-the-fly 
conversion techniques Using redundant number representations simplifies the design and shortens 
the operation time. On-the-fly conversion techniques are used to improve the performance of the 
algorithm by quickly correcting the error during the iteration process. The design based on the SRT4 
algorithm mentioned by Jiyang Chen employs these techniques [9]. 
4. 
Evaluation of hardware implementation methods 
The hardware architecture and design consider different division algorithms for different application 
scenarios. For example, Ziyang Deng proposed that the SRT-8 algorithm is widely used in the design 
of floating-point dividers because of its fast iteration speed [10].The CORDIC algorithm, on the other 
hand, is suitable for FPGA implementation of complex dividers due to its rotation operation instead 
of multiplication and addition operation. The Radix-8 algorithm improves the speed of the complex 
divider and reduces the use of hardware resources by means of a bit-by-bit recursive algorithm and 
an operand pre-transformation technique. Tzu-Coc Deng proposed that hardware architectures for 
high-performance dividers are usually SIMD structures , parallel structures or optimized structures 
based on specific algorithms. These architectures are designed to increase computing speed and 
reduce power consumption. When designing a high-performance divider, Deng Ziyi needs to consider 
how to optimize the iterative division structure, how to reduce the hardware resource overhead, and 
how to improve the speed and accuracy of the operation .Advantages, Disadvantages and Applicable 
Scenarios of Different Hardware Implementation Methods SRT-8 algorithm, the advantage is that the 
iteration speed is fast and it is suitable for the design of a floating-point divider, the disadvantage is 
that it may require larger hardware resources. Jingcun Wang proposed the CORDIC algorithm with 
the advantages of device saving, high computational accuracy, and applicability to FPGA 
implementation of complex divider, and the disadvantage that it may not be applicable to all types of 
division operations. The Radix-8 algorithm, has the advantage of increased speed and reduced 
hardware resources, and the disadvantage that complex re-transformation techniques may be required.

implementation. The CORDIC (Coordinate Rotation Digital Computer) algorithm has a wide range 
of applications in FPGA implementations of complex dividers, especially in the field of digital signal 
processing (DSP).The CORDIC algorithm implements multiplication and division of complex 
numbers through a series of rotational operations, which significantly reduces the hardware resources 
required and improves the speed of operations compared to the traditional multiplication and division 
operations. Specifically for the complex divider application case, the CORDIC algorithm is used as 
an alternative to the traditional multiplication and addition operations. In complex division, the 
CORDIC algorithm adjusts the angle of the complex numbers through a rotation operation to achieve 
the division operation. Wang Yingbo suggests that the advantage of this approach is that it requires 
only basic addition, subtraction and shift operations without the need for complex multipliers or 
lookup tables, which greatly simplifies the hardware design and reduces resource consumption. For 
performance evaluation, implementations of CORDIC algorithms on FPGA typically exhibit high 
computational speed and low hardware resource consumption. For example, in the design of a 
complex divider based on the CORDIC algorithm, the multiplication and addition operations are 
replaced by using the CORDIC rotation operation, and the result is finally obtained by two shift 
operations. In addition, an improved version of the CORDIC algorithm further optimizes the 
performance of the algorithm. For example, by improving the judgement equations for the single 
iteration angle and the currently selected angle, the number of iterations can be reduced while 
maintaining the same computational accuracy, thus increasing the speed of the FFT operation. This 
improvement not only increases the efficiency of the algorithm, but also reduces the hardware area 
consumption and improves the computational accuracy. 
In graphics processors, floating-point dividers are used to perform complex graphics rendering 
algorithms such as ray tracing and shadow calculations. In digital signal processing, dividers are used 
for tasks such as filter design and signal analysis. In addition, Huimin Du proposed that high 
performance dividers are also used in embedded systems and mobile devices to increase processing 
speed and reduce power consumption. Performance evaluation typically includes metrics such as 
computing speed, accuracy, area, and power consumption. Computing speed is usually measured in 
terms of the number of floating point operations performed per second (FLOPS).Accuracy, on the 
other hand, is assessed by comparing the difference between the calculated result and the actual value, 
and commonly used error metrics include ULP(unit in the last position).Tina Ho mentioned that area 
and power consumption, on the other hand, are important metrics for measuring the cost of hardware 
implementation, especially important in mobile and embedded devices. These data show that different 
algorithms and design strategies can significantly affect the performance of the divider. The results 
of the performance evaluation are important for the design and implementation of the divider. Firstly, 
they help designers to select or optimize algorithms to meet the needs of a particular application. 
Secondly, by comparing the performance of different designs, the allocation and optimization of 
hardware resources can be guided. Finally, performance evaluation results can also be used to predict 
how a new design will perform in real-world applications, thereby accelerating the product 
development process. In conclusion, performance evaluation of high-performance dividers is a 
multidimensional process involving a variety of techniques and methods. By continuously optimizing 
the algorithms and design, the performance of the divider can be significantly improved to meet the 
increasing computational demands. 
The latest use cases of high performance dividers in the field of graphics processing and digital 
signal processing are mainly in the following areas.3D image processing algorithm that implements 
a three-stage pipeline divider, which is a new type of divider with smaller area and faster speed than 
the traditional divider while satisfying the same accuracy. Digital signal processing (DSP) 
multiplication is one of the main operations. For example, novel approximate 4:2 compressors based

The main technical challenges faced by high performance dividers are accuracy control. As the 
computational demands increase, so do the accuracy requirements for the divider. For example, 
Tingting He proposes that floating-point dividers need to support the IEEE-754 standard, which 
requires the dividers to ensure the accuracy of the computation results along with the speed [1].In 
addition, approximate computational methods, while reducing power consumption and design 
complexity, may sacrifice some computational accuracy. Power consumption optimization, as 
semiconductor technology evolves, the performance gains from traditional scaling effects gradually 
diminish and power consumption issues become a key challenge in design. High-performance 
dividers need to guarantee performance while keeping power consumption as low as possible. Lidong 
Xing proposed, for example, an FPGA-based low-power high-speed divider design that significantly 
reduces dynamic power consumption by using new algorithms and gated clocking 
techniques .Algorithm optimization requires continuous exploration and optimization of the division 
algorithm. For example, a divider based on the SRT algorithm improves the speed of integer and 
floating-point division operations by optimizing the design structure. In addition, a double-precision 
floating-point divider based on Goldschmidt's algorithm achieves higher performance through 
improved algorithms and hardware multiplexing methods. 
5. 
Future development trends 
The future development trend of high-performance separator new materials and new processes will 
be more efficient and energy-saving applications. For example, a new high-frequency, high-linearity 
CMOS cross-conductivity current-mode multiplier/divider utilizes an advanced CMOS process to 
improve bandwidth and linearity while reducing power consumption. The development of novel 
algorithms has become an important direction for the future. For example, a new divider based on a 
two-bit algorithm significantly improves the speed of the division operation by reducing the number 
of execution cycles. In addition, the 64-bit divider, designed based on the principles of bead work, 
utilizes the principles of the operating model of ancient mathematics to significantly reduce the 
critical path delay. Integrator for hardware accelerators have become a trend. Weisheng Wang 
proposed, for example, a single-precision Goldschmidt divider integrated into a SOC based on the 
Cortex-M3 core, which effectively improves the speed of the division operation in the image 
recognition process . 
6. 
Conclusion 
This paper comprehensively discusses the design of high-performance divider, the research 
significance of which is to enhance the performance of integer and floating-point division operations 
in microprocessors, which is crucial for high-performance computing, digital signal processing, 
communication systems, image processing and other key areas. Through in-depth analysis and 
comparison of different division algorithms, this paper reveals the advantages and limitations of 
various algorithms and proposes an optimized design structure to meet the needs of different 
application scenarios. The results show that by optimizing the algorithm and design, the performance 
of the divider can be significantly improved to meet the increasing computational demands.

Looking ahead, the trend in high-performance dividers will focus on the application of new 
materials and processes, the development of novel algorithms, and the integration of hardware 
accelerators. With the development of new materials and processes, the design of high-performance 
dividers will become more efficient and energy-saving. The development of novel algorithms will 
respond to increasing computational demands, while the integration of hardware accelerators will 
improve computational efficiency in specific application scenarios. These advances will not only 
promote the technological progress in related fields, but also provide effective technical support for 
practical applications, foreshadowing a brighter future for high-performance divider design.

In the field of high-performance computing (HPC) and scientific computing, the design of floating-point divisors is critical because division is one of the most complex operations in floating-point arithmetic. The article firstly introduces the standard and arithmetic rules of floating-point numbers, analyses the basic principles of floating-point division, and compares the advantages and disadvantages of several classical floating-point division algorithms. In particular, the design of a double-precision floating- point divider based on Goldschmidt's algorithm is investigated in order to solve the problem of the complexity of the double-precision floating-point division arithmetic process and the large delay. The article also discusses current technology trends and practical application requirements for high-performance divider design, including applications in digital signal processing, communication systems, image processing, and other fields. In addition, the article discusses key factors such as the selection of the initial value of the iteration, the determination of the number of iterations, and the error control, and evaluates the advantages and disadvantages of different hardware implementations such as the SRT algorithm, the CORDIC algorithm, and the Radix-8 algorithm. Finally, the article looks at future trends in high-performance dividers, including the application of new materials and processes, the development of novel algorithms, and the integration of hardware accelerators.
